lessons.title: The Five Oceans
lessons.notes_html:
There are five oceans on the Earth's surface: the Pacific Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Antarctic (Southern) Ocean and the Arctic Ocean. An ocean is an excessively vast and deep body of saltish water. The oceans and seas hold 97 percent of the world's total water.

The Three Largest Oceans

  • Pacific Ocean — the largest ocean, with an area of 168 million sq. km, covering 45% of the world's oceanic surface. It is also the deepest ocean, with an average depth of 4,200 metres. The Mariana Trench in it, about 11 km deep, is the deepest place on the ocean floor.
  • Atlantic Ocean — the second largest ocean, covering 29% of the world's oceanic surface, with an area of 85 million sq. km and an average depth of 3,650 metres. Its deepest point is the Puerto Rico Trench, 8,648 metres deep, and it lies in the earthquake-active zones of the world.
  • Indian Ocean — the third largest ocean, with an area of 70 million sq. km, which is 20% of the world's oceanic surface. Its average depth is 3,900 metres, it extends mostly in the Southern Hemisphere, and its deepest point is the Java Trench, 7,400 metres deep.

The Arctic Ocean is the smallest ocean of the world; in this book its area is given as 15 million sq. km. The Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean Sea.

lessons.title: Bays, Gulfs, Islands and Peninsulas
lessons.notes_html:
A bay is a long and wide part of an ocean that penetrates into the land. Like a gulf, a bay is also enclosed by land on three sides. Examples are the Bay of Bengal and Hudson Bay. A gulf is a large and narrow portion of the ocean that penetrates the land.

Island and Peninsula

  • An island is a piece of land surrounded by water on all sides, for example Astola Island near Gwadar.
  • A peninsula is a piece of land surrounded by water on three sides, for example the Arabian Peninsula, the Deccan Peninsula and the Indo-China Peninsula.

The aquatic plants and animals consumed by human beings are called seafood.

lessons.title: Importance of Oceans in Our Lives
lessons.notes_html:
Oceans are important in our lives in many ways. They produce oxygen which helps us in breathing: plankton, a microscopic plant in the oceans, produces more than 50 percent of the oxygen available on Earth.

Climate, Economy and Food

  • Oceans regulate the Earth's climate because they absorb heat from the sun and so help maintain the Earth's surface temperature.
  • They serve as a lifeline for most of the world's economy, facilitating job creation, tourism, fishing and international shipping.
  • Many items of medicinal value are extracted from the oceans.
  • The oceans are an important source of food for human beings, and they are home to several species of plants and animals.

We get roughly 140 million tons of seafood annually, much of it fish. Seafood contains high amounts of nutrients, important minerals, vitamins and fatty acids, and it has less negative impact on the climate than land-based agriculture. To keep receiving these benefits, fish and other aquatic resources should be used in a sustainable manner.

lessons.title: Marine Biodiversity
lessons.notes_html:
Marine biodiversity means the species living in the oceans; it includes all animals, plants and microorganisms. The ocean is one of the major habitats of world biodiversity, accounting for over 90 percent of the habitable space on Earth.

Why Marine Biodiversity Matters

  • Marine species supply half of the oxygen we breathe.
  • The oceans absorb about 20 percent of the annual human-made carbon dioxide emitted into the atmosphere, so they keep the Earth's systems working healthily.
  • Hundreds of millions of people are connected with the fishery and aquatic sector, and marine biodiversity contributes directly and indirectly to food security.
  • Marine ecosystems provide services to people living in coastal areas, such as livelihoods, clean water and forest products.

Marine biodiversity is therefore important for the economic, social and environmental aspects of sustainable development.

lessons.title: Threats to the Oceans and Climate Change
lessons.notes_html:
Human activities are the main threat to ocean health. About 80 percent of marine pollution comes from direct human activities.

Threats to the Oceans

  • Factories and industrial plants release sewage and cause oil spills.
  • Fertilizers and pesticides used in agriculture end up in coastal waters, lower the oxygen and destroy marine life.
  • About eight million tons of plastic enter the seas every year.
  • Intensive fishing depletes resources and threatens ecosystems.
  • Rising sea levels due to global warming threaten the coasts.

Climate Change and the Oceans

Climate change is causing serious changes in the oceans, such as sea level rise, temperature increase, changes in ocean currents and acidification. As global temperatures rise, polar ice caps and glaciers are melting, which increases sea levels; the rise in sea level causes erosion and coastal flooding and affects marine biodiversity. The melting ice is also leading to the loss of habitat for polar species. Oceans are becoming more acidic as they absorb more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and at the same time oxygen levels are decreasing.

lessons.notes_html:
Weather is the daily atmospheric condition of a place — its temperature, humidity, rainfall, etc. It is assumed for an hour, a day, a month or even a year.

Climate is the average weather condition of a region observed over a long period of time. The climate of a region is usually tracked for at least 30 years.

Weather and climate are different: weather is the short-term condition of the atmosphere at a place, while climate describes the long-term average pattern of that place. For example, Karachi experiences a tropical climate.

lessons.title: Extreme Weather Events
lessons.notes_html:
Extreme weather events are weather events that are different from normal weather events. They cause harm to the people and their property, and because of climate change their intensity and frequency are increasing each year worldwide.

Examples from the Unit

  • Heat waves: a severe heat wave of 49 degrees Celsius struck southern Pakistan in June 2015 and caused the deaths of more than 1,500 people.
  • Cyclones: a cyclone is a powerful storm containing rain and strong winds. In May 1999 a cyclone struck Keti Bandar, Thatta district, Sindh, killing 6,200 people and destroying 75,000 houses.
  • Drought: a prolonged dry period in the natural climate cycle that can last for months or years. Pakistan faced the worst drought in 1998 and 2002, and Balochistan has a long history of droughts affecting its economy, livelihoods, agriculture and livestock.
  • Heavy rainfall: a high amount of rainfall in a short period causes flash flooding. In 2022 most areas of Sindh, Balochistan and southern Punjab suffered severe floods which killed about 1,739 people, affected 33 million people and damaged 1.7 million homes.
  • Strong winds and cold spell: the Murree snowstorm of 7 January 2022 dropped more than 4 feet of snow and took the lives of 23 tourists.

lessons.title: Global Warming and the Causes of Climate Change
lessons.notes_html:
Global warming is the rise in the average temperature of the Earth. The Earth's average temperature has increased by 1 degree Celsius over the past 100 years, mainly because human activities such as burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas) release greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Greenhouse gases trap the sun's heat in the atmosphere. Important greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone.

Main Causes of Climate Change

  • Greenhouse gases released by human activities, which raise the Earth's temperature.
  • Industrial activities, which since the Industrial Revolution have released large amounts of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide as smoke.
  • Deforestation, because trees absorb carbon dioxide, and when forests are cut the stored carbon dioxide is released back; deforestation is responsible for 15% of the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.
  • Transportation, which burns fossil fuels and releases massive amounts of carbon dioxide and other pollutants.
  • Agriculture, because rearing animals produces methane and nitrogen fertilizers produce nitrous oxide.

Oil drilling and volcanic eruptions are also causes of climate change.

lessons.title: Effects of Climate Change on Human Life
lessons.notes_html:
Climate change affects human life in many ways, through more frequent and severe droughts, rising sea levels, melting glaciers, floods, forest fires and heat waves. It threatens human health, safety and food production, particularly in developing countries.

Three Major Threats

  • The global temperature has risen due to increased greenhouse gas emissions, causing heat waves that harm human health, agriculture and ecosystems.
  • Extreme weather events such as droughts, floods, cyclones and wildfires are becoming more frequent and severe, harming lives and property.
  • The melting of ice caps and glaciers is raising the sea level, causing coastal flooding and erosion and threatening coastal populations, infrastructure and plants.

Effects on Health, Food and Farming

  • Health: rising temperatures and heat waves can lead to heatstroke, heat exhaustion and dehydration, and respiratory problems such as asthma; climate change also impacts water quality and availability.
  • Food supply: climate change affects water scarcity, agricultural production, crop yields, livestock health, fisheries and food security.
  • Farming: rising temperatures negatively affect crop productivity and quality, pests and diseases spread more easily in hot conditions, and heavy rainfall or intense storms increase the risk of soil erosion and degradation.

There is a close connection between climate change and extreme weather: warm air holds more moisture, which leads to greater rainfall and stronger storms, and coastal flooding has become more common as a result of sea level rise. People living in the coastal areas of Balochistan are mainly linked with fishing, so rising sea level, which leads to coastal flooding, directly threatens their lives.

lessons.title: Life in River Plains, Tropical and Polar Regions
lessons.notes_html:
River plains are a vast expanse of fertile land, ideal for agricultural purposes. People living in these plains rely on farming as their primary livelihood and cultivate crops such as rice, wheat, corn and vegetables, using the sufficient water supply for irrigation. River plains are rich in biodiversity, and rivers have historically been used as natural transportation corridors.

Tropical Regions

Tropical regions lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn on both sides of the equator. The climate is hot and humid and people wear light clothing. In tropical rainforests, which receive 1,800 mm to 2,500 mm of rainfall each year, people rely on their surroundings for food, shelter and medicines and are involved in cutting trees for wood, fishing, rubber plantation and agriculture. In tropical deserts, where rainfall is low and temperatures are the highest on Earth, most people lead a nomadic life and rear animals such as camels, horses, sheep and goats.

Polar Regions

In polar regions, winters are long and dark, summers are short with 24 hours of daylight, and temperatures often drop below minus 30 degrees Celsius. People there wear thick clothes and eat warm food to protect themselves from the cold, live a nomadic life, and live in houses of snow called igloos. Sledges are used for transportation and the reindeer is common, while farming and mining are very difficult because of the extreme cold.

lessons.title: The Environment and Its Spheres
lessons.notes_html:
The environment means the surroundings in which we live. It consists of both living and non-living components. The Earth has more than two-thirds of its surface covered with water.

Two Types of Environment

  • Natural environment, which consists of living and non-living things occurring naturally, like water, plants, land and air.
  • Man-made environment, where humans modify their surroundings according to their own needs, for example houses, roads and cars.

The Four Spheres of the Natural Environment

  • Atmosphere — the layer of air around the Earth.
  • Lithosphere — the top hard layer of the Earth.
  • Hydrosphere — the water part of the Earth.
  • Biosphere — the sphere made up of plants and animals.

The ozone layer is a layer in the stratosphere that contains a high concentration of ozone (O3) molecules. Depletion of the ozone layer affects life on the Earth.

lessons.title: Pollution and Its Types
lessons.notes_html:
Pollution is harmful material in the environment. These harmful materials are called pollutants, and the presence of these pollutants in our environment is called environmental pollution. Human activities are the primary cause of most of the pollution on Earth.

Types of Pollution

  • Water pollution is the contamination of water sources by chemicals, trash or microorganisms, making water unusable for drinking, cooking and swimming; contamination of drinking water causes diseases like diarrhea, cholera, dysentery and typhoid.
  • Land pollution is the unwanted physical or chemical change in the composition and structure of the soil, caused by dumping trash, toxic industrial and domestic waste and chemical fertilizers and pesticides; it makes soil infertile.
  • Air pollution is the mixing of harmful gases, dust and smoke with the air, caused by burning fossil fuels, industrialization and deforestation; it causes respiratory diseases, acid rain and global warming.
  • Noise pollution is unpleasant and undesirable sound from loudspeakers, automobiles and airplanes.
  • Light pollution is excessive, unsuitable or misdirected artificial lighting, which hides the night sky.

All types of pollution are caused mainly by human activities and harm the environment, but each affects a different part of it.

Causes of Water Pollution

lessons.title: Greenhouse Gases, Global Warming and the Ozone Layer
lessons.notes_html:
Greenhouse gases are a certain percentage of gases present in the atmosphere. The main greenhouse gases named in the unit are methane (CH4), ozone (O3) and carbon dioxide (CO2); nitrous oxide and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are also counted among them.

Greenhouse gases trap the sun's heat and stop it from going back into space, creating the greenhouse effect. Global warming is the rise in the Earth's surface temperature caused by the imbalance in the composition of greenhouse gases: as the amount of these gases increases, they trap more heat and the Earth's temperature rises. Human activities such as burning fossil fuels are raising their concentration in the atmosphere.

Effects of Greenhouse Gases

  • They cause climate change by trapping heat, which is global warming.
  • They also cause ocean acidification.
  • They contribute to health impacts, including respiratory diseases from smog and air pollution.
  • Extreme weather events, food supply disruptions and the disruption of ecosystems are other effects.
  • The release of harmful gases such as CFCs causes ozone layer depletion, which does not stop the harmful rays coming from the sun and can cause skin diseases in humans.

lessons.notes_html:
Preventing Ozone Layer Depletion

  • Avoid the consumption of gases dangerous to the ozone layer, such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and nitrous oxide.
  • Minimize the usage of vehicles that produce more greenhouse gases.
  • Use eco-friendly home appliances such as air conditioners and refrigerators and conduct their regular maintenance.
  • Raise public campaigns and awareness about the importance of the ozone layer.
  • Encourage the development and use of natural and eco-friendly substitutes.
  • Promote the use of renewable energy sources to reduce the demand for burning fossil fuels.

Reducing Different Types of Pollution

  • Establish industrial zones away from urban areas.
  • Reduce automobiles and regularly maintain and check them.
  • End the burning of wood, leaves and garbage, which are sources of air pollution.
  • Use eco-friendly chemicals for domestic, industrial and agricultural purposes.
  • Dispose of unwanted medications properly to protect people, pets and the environment.
  • Reduce deforestation and increase trees, which helps us get fresh air.
  • Recycle plastic wastes such as bags, bottles and cans.
  • Turn off unused lights, appliances and equipment.

lessons.title: Major Industries of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan is a developing country with a diverse range of industries. Five main industries of Pakistan are: (1) textile industry, (2) fertilizer industry, (3) sugar industry, (4) cement industry, and (5) chemical industry. The automobile, steel and iron industries are also major industries of Pakistan.

Important Industries

  • Textile industry is the biggest industry of Pakistan and the backbone of its economy: Pakistan earns about 55% of its foreign exchange from it, almost 42% of industrial workers are engaged in it, and Karachi is its hub, with Faisalabad the second most important centre.
  • Cement industry uses limestone and gypsum, which are available in large reserves in the country; its centres include Karachi, Hyderabad, Dandot, Dera Ghazi Khan and Kohat.
  • Sugar industry has grown from only two sugar mills at independence to many mills producing over 6 million metric tons of sugar per annum, with centres such as Mardan, Charsadda, Kamalia and Mirpur Khas.
  • Automobile industry is one of the fastest growing industries, manufacturing trucks, buses, cars, jeeps, auto-rickshaws, motorcycles and tractors in collaboration with China, Japan and Korea.
  • Sports goods industry is mostly located in Sialkot, and the leather industry produces good quality finished leather of international standard; both earn foreign exchange.

lessons.title: Increasing Exports, Science and Technology, and Economic Stability

How Pakistan Can Increase Its Exports

  • Enhance value addition in the export sector and simplify export regulations.
  • Improve the tourism industry, which will attract tourists.
  • Improve domestic goods' productivity and technological content according to international standards.
  • Urban development and good infrastructure are the backbone of the economic sector.
  • Explore more markets around the world, maintain the quality of local products according to international standards, meet the time schedules of trade partners and keep prices competitive.

Role of Science and Technology

Science and technology play the primary role in the industrial development of a country. Technology is the key to reducing unit costs, improving product quality, market share, output and profits. In Pakistan, science and technology has brought a modern media style, better marketing, distance learning programs and software technology services at national and international level. Modern technology such as drones and robots can help the agriculture sector, and tools such as artificial intelligence (AI), geographic information system (GIS) and remote sensing (RS) can be used for the development of different sectors.

Economic Stability

A nation with a stable economy is better equipped to withstand external shocks like trade disputes, and its resilience guarantees that the country can continue to provide basic services and sustain its people in difficult times. International trade is linked together by an effective and complex transport system, so an effective transport system has an important role in international trade. Major Trade Routes

  • Karachi Port — one of the busiest ports of South Asia, handling about 50% of the containerized cargo of the country; items like iron ore, coal, steel, edible oil, grains, cement and agricultural products are exported and imported through it.
  • Port Qasim — handles mineral oils, edible oil, coal, rice, wheat, cement, fertilizers, general cargo, containers and LNG.
  • Gwadar Port — a deep-sea port developed with the help of China under CPEC, becoming the gateway port for Pakistan and the region.
  • Karakoram Highway (Silk Route) — the Silk Road of the twenty-first century, connecting Pakistan and China through the Khunjerab Pass; Pakistan exports agricultural products, textiles and seafood to China, while China occupies the largest share in Pakistan's total imports.
  • Chaman and Torkham borders — trade with Afghanistan; Pakistan exports cement, fruits, vegetables, cold drinks and construction materials, and imports dry fruit and fresh vegetables. Chaman is the border town in Balochistan.
  • Taftan border — the point where Quetta is connected with Iran by rail and road.

Transport Infrastructure: Strengths and Weaknesses

Its strengths are: the expanding and upgrading road network has connected urban and rural areas and made the movement of goods easy; projects like CPEC have led to the construction of modern roads, improving connectivity and trade; development of transport infrastructure has reduced the cost of goods; the transport system provides job opportunities and opens up investment opportunities in less developed areas. Its weaknesses are: inadequate and weak infrastructure, which causes delays of goods, increased transportation costs and damage to goods; lack of implementation of traffic rules; lack of well-maintained roads; security challenges; old or outdated vehicles; and traffic congestion, lack of parking spaces and illegal encroachment.

lessons.title: The Human Development Index (HDI)
lessons.notes_html:
The Human Development Index (HDI) was introduced in 1990 by the United Nations and is published under the UNDP. It is a summary measure of average achievement in the key aspects of human development.

The Three Indicators of HDI

  • A healthy life, measured by life expectancy at birth, which is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live.
  • Education, measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling.
  • A decent standard of living, measured by Gross National Income (GNI) per capita.

Pakistan has made steady progress in improving its HDI since the early 1990s. According to the Human Development Report 2022, Pakistan's HDI rank is 161 out of 192 countries. This low rank shows that Pakistan still stands among the less developed countries and needs improvement in income, jobs, education and health to raise its position.

EDI and HDI Compared

Both EDI and HDI measure the development of a country. Economic Development Indicators (EDI) show the economic well-being of a region in money and production terms, while HDI measures the overall well-being of its people. In short, EDI measures the economy of a country, while HDI measures the overall well-being of its people.

lessons.title: The OECD and the Role of Technology in Development
lessons.notes_html:
The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) is an international organization founded in 1961 that works to stimulate economic progress and world trade. It has 38 member countries collaborating to develop policy standards to promote sustainable economic growth.

Role and Objectives of the OECD

  • For more than 60 years it has been a reliable source of evidence-based policy analysis and economic data.
  • It provides a setting where governments can compare experiences, seek answers to common challenges, identify good practices, and develop high standards for economic policy.
  • It supports development in developing countries through knowledge sharing, capacity building, efforts in good governance and anti-corruption, policy advice and support for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
  • In Pakistan, the OECD plays a major role in sectors such as education, skills development, economic growth, policy making, revenue and taxation and international trade.

Role of Technology in Development

Technology is the use of scientific knowledge for practical goals, and it is a changing agent in economic development. It can drive economic growth by increasing productivity, efficiency and innovation, and can create new industries and job opportunities, leading to higher income and overall economic prosperity. It supports environmental sustainability through renewable energy sources, sustainable agricultural methods and waste management solutions, helps build infrastructure such as energy sources, communication networks and transportation systems, and can improve the educational system by providing new educational tools.
